people.name: Jack Carter
people.summary: Jack Carter started at the club cleaning members’ clubs as a twelve-year-old in 1957. After playing in Canada and returning to the Bay, he found himself organising Sunday junior golf. He recalls finding a new use for the Spalding Cup, turning it into the prize for a mixed under-19 tournament whose fields included future professionals.

people.name: Alison Holdem
people.summary: Alison Holdem learned golf on a sheep and cattle farm at Pyes Pā, where she later won the Ngawaro senior championship. She joined Tauranga in 1985, worked with Phyll Sandlant on the nine-hole programme from 1998 and took over as convenor when Phyll retired from the role.

people.name: Adrienne Coad
people.summary: Adrienne Coad helped Tauranga’s beginners learn the game and earn a handicap, with Hazel Casey assisting her. In 2010 she and Beryl Smith volunteered to keep the women’s summer golf programme going after Connie Breeds retired. A 2020 club newsletter records Adrienne still teaching the game, leading a weekly rules group for nine-hole and 18-hole players.

people.name: Jackie Reynish
people.summary: Jackie Reynish researched the people and stories behind Tauranga’s trophies, including awards that were no longer presented. She compiled two albums, one for current trophies and one for archived ones, with photographs and details of who presented each trophy. The September 2020 club newsletter pointed members to both albums in the meeting room.

people.name: Chris McAlpine
people.summary: Chris McAlpine played in Tauranga’s intermediate pennant team in 2003, the year the club won the senior, intermediate and junior titles. He also worked in regional golf administration. Jack Carter recalls working alongside Chris as Bay of Plenty Golf’s chief executive while managing the senior men’s team.

people.name: Anne Mark
people.summary: Anne Mark carried her experience at Tauranga into national golf administration. In 1960, as a member of the Ladies’ Golf Union executive, she sent the club news of a change to scorecard requirements. Members also knew her as a player and team manager, one of several ways she helped shape women’s golf both at home and beyond the club.

people.name: Una Wickham
people.summary: Una Wickham won 16 senior club championships and took Tauranga golf onto the national stage, winning the 1959 national foursomes with fellow member Olga Johnson. The women’s match-play tournament later took Una’s name, commemorating her through an event that drew leading players from across the North Island.

people.name: Evelyn (Nen) Sim
people.summary: In 1974, Nen Sim became the first woman elected to the club executive. That same summer she led the twilight catering volunteers. Her records show them feeding 70 people on one January evening in 1975, serving roast chicken, corned beef and salads for a dollar a head. The proceeds later helped equip the clubhouse kitchen.

people.name: Dick Phelan
people.summary: Dick Phelan won the senior club championship in 1930 and reached a junior championship final 47 years later. Between those two finals he helped turn friendly weekday golf into an organised fixture, serving as the Veterans’ Golfing Society’s first secretary in 1952.

people.name: George Willcock
people.summary: George Wilcock was among the golfers whose friendly postwar rounds laid the foundations for the Veterans’ Golfing Society. He went on to serve as club president from 1950 to 1952. His name also lives on in the Wilcock Cup, a handicap match-play event for intermediate men.

people.name: Arthur Towsey
people.summary: Arthur Towsey served on the committee and volunteered to run the bar, where Mowat remembers him as an accomplished host who kept order with a flexible touch. He was also one of the golfers who gathered for friendly weekday rounds after the war. Those rounds grew into the Veterans’ Golfing Society.

people.name: Harry Bradmore
people.summary: Harry Bradmore and his son Maurice planted and tended young trees around the course, carrying on the work begun by Alick Mirrielees. Harry also encouraged young golfers, giving Mary Parkinson a book on the game when she was starting out. He presented the Alan Bradmore Memorial Trophy in memory of another son, who died in the Second World War.

people.name: James Mowat
people.summary: James Mowat arrived in 1936 as Tauranga’s first professional. His appointment came as the club was reshaping the course and looking to improve the standard of play. He taught golfers, worked on their equipment and helped bring on a generation of younger players at Gate Pā.

people.name: David Mowat
people.summary: Before editing the club’s centenary history, Dave Mowat had already spent decades helping run the club. He was captain in 1969 and 1970, went on to the presidency, and returned to serve as board chair from 1999. For the book he brought earlier research, club records and members’ recollections together in time for the 2014 centenary at Gate Pā.

people.name: Elsie Hanna
people.summary: Before the clubhouse had much of a kitchen, Elsie Hanna helped feed visiting teams with water heated in an outdoor bath and kettles on spirit burners. Fellow member Margaret remembered her potato salad especially fondly. Elsie also won two senior championships and became the club’s first woman Life Member.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Noel Copestake
people.summary: Noel Copestake’s time as president took him onto the club’s first Board of Management in 1994. Away from the boardroom he promoted twilight golf, helped select and manage pennant teams and led the Wednesday Firewood Gang. In 2005 he and Peg became the first married couple in the club’s published roll to both hold Life Membership.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Bernie Child
people.summary: Bernie Child put his experience with heavy machinery to work on the veterans’ course projects. One smaller job was entirely his own: he built the drinking fountain behind the first tee and added a plaque that played on his surname. In 1995 he took on the presidency of the Veterans’ Golfing Society.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Hazel Casey
people.summary: At eleven, Hazel Casey learned golf on a farm course near Ōpōtiki where cows kept the fairways short and her first subscription was five fruit tins to line the holes. At Tauranga she helped beginners earn their handicaps, organised raffles to pay for lessons and took charge of the Saturday women’s nine-hole group.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Ernie Craig
people.summary: When a council subcommittee proved ineffective at running the Racecourse Reserve, Ernie Craig pushed for a committee that could work directly with its tenants and put rents back into maintaining the grounds. He served on the reserve’s governing bodies for more than 50 years. Both the golf and racing clubs awarded him Life Membership.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Peg Copestake
people.summary: Before taking up golf, Peg Copestake competed as Peggy Smith in hockey, table tennis, indoor basketball and athletics. Within about five years of starting golf, a Bay of Plenty Times clipping records her winning the South Auckland women’s championship and playing off a handicap of one. She later took a trailer of golf equipment to local schools to teach children the game and became the first woman elected president of Tauranga Golf Club.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

features.alt: Peg Copestake standing beside her golf trolley
features.caption: An early photograph of Peg Copestake. Date and photographer unrecorded. Supplied by Bruce Partridge.

features.title: From Peggy Smith to a one-handicap golfer
paragraphs: The clipping recalls that Peg represented Auckland in hockey and Bay of Plenty in table tennis, reached the national mixed doubles semi-finals, and placed third in the discus at the New Zealand championships. It also describes how she spent her first three months with golf coach Bronco Branch on lessons and practice before playing on a course. By the time of the article, she had won the South Auckland women’s championship and the J. W. Ellis Challenge Cup in a field of 64.

The clipping has no visible publication date. The article says Peg had started playing about five years earlier and had yet to win a Tauranga club championship. Dave Mowat records that she joined Tauranga in 1961, and the club’s honour roll lists her first senior title in 1974. These clues suggest the mid-1960s, with the exact issue still unconfirmed.
features.alt: Newspaper clipping about Peg Copestake’s early sporting and golfing career
features.caption: “Do You Remember …”, attributed to the Bay of Plenty Times, signed J.M. Undated clipping supplied by Bruce Partridge.

people.name: H B Lusk
people.summary: When the club moved to the Racecourse Reserve in 1914, H. B. Lusk helped work out how to lay out a golf course on the new ground. Members then had to turn the reserve’s rough pasture into playable holes. The club recognised his contribution with Life Membership in 1948–49.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: A J Mirrielees
people.summary: A pharmacist and keen photographer, Alick Mirrielees recorded the early Domain golfers in photographs that still illustrate the club’s history. After the move to Gate Pā, he helped plant a wide variety of trees on the reserve. The plantings changed how the course looked and how golfers played it.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Phyll Sandlant
people.summary: When Phyll Sandlant invited women to try nine-hole golf in February 1998, 96 signed up on the first call. She and the volunteers arranged coaching with Rick Barker, then walked a few holes with the beginners so they could put the lessons into practice. That first intake helped establish a regular nine-hole programme at Tauranga.
people.source: Life Members Landscape.pdf; existing heritage profile supplied 10 November 2026

people.name: Keith Dawkins
people.summary: Keith Dawkins came to golf from cricket with a grip that raised eyebrows. It served him well enough to win four senior club championships in five years from 1963 to 1967. He later served as captain and volunteered for another term in 1995 when the club had trouble finding someone to take the job.

people.name: Maurice White
people.summary: Maurice White spent much of his time on the club committee chairing finance, sometimes as the finance committee’s only member. He became an early advocate for a Board of Management and helped work out the constitutional details that allowed the club to make the change in 1994.

people.name: Mike Sandlant
people.summary: Long-time mate and club stalwart, pictured with Keith Dawkins and Jack Carter.

people.name: Joyce Paris
people.summary: Board chairperson in the 1990s and one of the first elected board members in November 1994. Also pictured sharing a Nancy McCormick foursomes triumph with Life Member Hazel Casey.
people.source: Pars from the Past (2014), pp. 106, 142; photograph and identification added 11 November 2026. Page 142 names Joyce as chairperson but gives a conflicting sequence for the handover to Barbara Glynn; the exact chair dates remain to be checked.

people.name: Joyce Edwards
people.summary: Joyce Edwards joined with her husband Roy in the mid-1950s and was soon keeping records and handicaps for the women’s club. She went on to captain the women, serve as their president and lead the regional association in 1978–79. Long after those years in office, she was still getting out to play a few holes.
people.source: Club heritage photograph and identification added 11 November 2026; celebration date not supplied

people.name: E T Baker
people.summary: An early photograph taken below The Elms catches E. T. Baker and H. B. Mountfort beside the Waikareao Estuary. Both played on the original Domain course, when the club’s only recorded asset in 1911 was a hand mower. Baker was among the first men awarded Life Membership. Mowat found little detail about the service behind that honour.

people.name: Bert Goulding
people.summary: Around 1920, Bert Goulding planted the Moreton Bay fig beside the clubhouse. He also supplied and tended two Canadian redwoods behind the Knoll. Members knew him as a golfer too: he won the senior club championship in 1933 and was among the club’s earliest Life Members.

people.name: Denis Ivory
people.summary: Denis Ivory was club president from 1936 to 1939, years that saw the arrival of professional James Mowat and the opening of the 1938 clubhouse. He was among the five men honoured with Life Membership before 1948. The surviving account gives his term of office but little detail about his individual contribution.

people.name: P H Roach
people.summary: P. H. Roach won the senior club championship in 1919, five years after the move to Gate Pā. He was one of five men honoured with Life Membership before 1948. The championship and the honour roll are the clearest surviving records of his place in the club’s early years.

people.name: C Steedman
people.summary: The club knew C. Steedman as Steedy and awarded him Life Membership in 1948–49, around the same time as H. B. Lusk and Arthur Towsey. By the time Dave Mowat assembled the club history, the people who remembered Steedman’s work had passed away. The book preserves his nickname and the honour.

people.name: Warwick Nicol
people.summary: Warwick Nicol worked as a bank accountant in Tauranga and spent many years as the club’s men’s handicapper. He was already serving as president of the Bay of Plenty District Golf Association when he took up the Tauranga presidency in 1958. The club made him a Life Member that year, before his retirement to Tirau.

people.name: Alan Davidson
people.summary: Alan Davidson helped put the Harris course plan into practice during his second term as club president. On tournament days he took on work that players rarely saw. For the Tauranga Open, he and fellow volunteers gave up their chance to play so they could check cards and post scores by hand in time for prizegiving.

people.name: Keith Nattrass
people.summary: Keith Nattrass joined the club committee in 1957 and was elected vice-president the following year. He served as president of both Tauranga and the Bay of Plenty District Golf Association before taking office as North Island vice-president of the New Zealand Golf Association in 1969.

people.name: John Hare
people.summary: As the golf club and racing club worked out how to share the reserve, John Hare helped reconcile their differences. He chaired the Racecourse Domain Board and stayed out of office in either tenant club to avoid a conflict of interest. He still found ways to help both, acting as honorary solicitor for the golfers and as timekeeper for the races.

people.name: Keith Frith
people.summary: On his daughter’s wedding day in 1968, Keith Frith’s friend Vince O’Connor talked him into playing the second round of the Nicoll Cup at dawn. Keith finished the competition 12 up against par over 36 holes. Members also knew him for seven consecutive years as captain and for coming back to fill the role when the club needed him again.

people.name: Alex Gallagher
people.summary: A surveyor by trade, Alex Gallagher brought careful lettering and a knack for organising information to the club’s hand-written scoreboards. At the Spalding Masters and PGA Championship he coordinated scores arriving from around the course. He also played in club competitions, winning the junior championship in 1989 after losing the previous year’s final.

people.name: Rennie Gordon
people.summary: Playing as Rennie Daines, she won three consecutive women’s club championships from 1920 to 1922. She later served as captain and president of the women’s club. By 1961, as Rennie Gordon, she was helping gather material for an early club history, some of which found its way into Mowat’s book.

people.name: Joyce Carnachan
people.summary: Joyce Carnachan joined in 1931 and went on to serve on the women’s committee and as women’s president. The book preserves both a photograph of her with a winter golf group and a reminder of her contribution to the grounds: she donated the jacaranda beside the fourth green.

people.name: Edna Galbally
people.summary: Edna Galbally came to Tauranga to teach at Ōtūmoetai and joined the club in 1943. She spent 23 years in roles that included secretary, handicapper and Saturday supervisor. Her encouragement reached individual players too: she introduced future club president Peg Copestake to the game.

volunteer_sections.title: Making a course and a clubhouse

entries.title: Members establish Gate Pa
entries.summary: Working bees cleared gorse, protected greens with fences, built stiles, planted trees and prepared greens. The tin shed, shared meals and collected firewood show the practical beginnings of club life.

entries.title: Hospitality before modern facilities
entries.summary: The women’s committee cleaned the shed and prepared food at home for visiting teams. Anne Mark recalled finding kindling and cutting firewood; Elsie Hanna’s catering work involved heating water outside and using small spirit burners.

entries.title: Members improve the greens
entries.summary: Groups of bankers, commercial travellers, Loan and Mercantile staff and insurance brokers undertook to enlarge and remake greens. These are early examples of professional networks contributing practical work.

entries.title: A voluntary keeper of the bar
entries.summary: Arthur Towsey’s long committee service and voluntary care of the bar formed part of the welcome members and visitors received.

entries.title: A regular programme of service
entries.summary: Mowat dates the routine annual projects programme to 1985 while recognising earlier individual contributions. Peter Steward’s album preserved the Society’s activities through calligraphy, photographs and painstaking retrospective work.

entries.title: Painting, equipment and coring
entries.summary: Work in 1985–87 included painting club rooms and shelters, maintaining ball washers, rebuilding first-tee surrounds, replacing bunker rakes and assisting with coring. Walter Tombleson and Peter Baveystock are remembered for regular coring help.

entries.title: Gardens, mowing equipment and course repairs
entries.summary: The 1988–91 lists include a Toro mower blade attachment, bark gardens, paths, tee surrounds, drainage, fences, markers and storm-damaged trees.

entries.title: Paths, practice nets and irrigation
entries.summary: Projects in 1992–95 included steps and paths, Vets’ Dell, bunker work, course furniture, practice nets and assistance with the new irrigation system.

entries.title: The caddie-car shed, 1996
entries.summary: Under President Ron Holden, the Society supplied materials, designed and built a caddie-car shed adjoining the greenkeeper’s building beside the practice range.

entries.title: Fabrication, drainage and upkeep
entries.summary: Later 1990s work included a mower roller, stormwater channels, paths and railings, irrigator equipment, a sliding sand-bin roof and care of gardens and car-park markings. Longrun Industries gifted cladding used in the clubhouse fascia.

entries.title: Funding and hands-on work, 2000–04
entries.summary: Contributions included $6,000 for paths in 2000, $4,500 towards an irrigator and junior golf in 2001, and $12,000 in 2002, all but $400 of the latter coming from the firewood team. Joe Carr did the woodworking for a lectern funded in 2004.

entries.title: Paths, tournament preparation and turf
entries.summary: Projects included course tidying for Carrus, coring, practice-net renovation, paths supervised by Denis Smith with planning by Peter Bourne, and turf-nursery support. Veterans helped lay Windsor Green stolons on the eighteenth and nursery.

volunteer_sections.title: The Firewood Gang and tree care

entries.title: Noel Copestake’s Wednesday team
entries.summary: Mowat associates the emergence of the Wednesday Firewood Gang with the mid-1990s project lists; he does not give a settled foundation date. The group also became known as Dad’s Army.

entries.title: Work and money returned to the club
entries.summary: Removing dead trees, trimming, clearing fallen branches, providing clubhouse firewood and selling wood combined cost savings with funds for projects. The book does not assign a total lifetime value to this work.

entries.title: Jim Swainson and Bernie Child
entries.summary: Jim Swainson’s tree-care skills and Bernie Child’s project organisation, equipment design and maintenance receive special recognition. Child’s drinking fountain behind the first tee was his own initiative and work.

entries.title: A landscape of donated trees
entries.summary: Planting and care involved A. J. Mirrielees, Harry and Maurice Bradmore, Fred Washer, Frank and Maisie Warnes and Willis Faulds. Bill Kennedy donated specimens despite not being a golfer; Bob Burstall contributed specialist tree knowledge.

entries.title: Paid work alongside donated effort
entries.summary: The book distinguishes relief workers, paid backpackers used in turf planting and contracted arboriculture from volunteering. It also says some clubhouse advisers were paid for professional services while donating meeting and site-visit time.

volunteer_sections.title: Women’s committees, hospitality and social life

entries.title: Anne Mark, Elsie Hanna and Nen Sim
entries.summary: Their work linked catering, handicapping, committee service and leadership. Nen’s contribution also included communication through the Bunkered newspaper column and development of the club’s social life.

entries.title: The women veterans’ contributions
entries.summary: Raffles, donated prizes, tournament organisation and sponsorship generated money for club facilities. The account records changing-room support, planter-box funding and a suggested handrail, as well as the work of successive committees.

entries.title: Summer golf organisers
entries.summary: After Connie Breeds stood down in 2010, Beryl Smith and Adrienne Coad volunteered to carry on the summer programme.

entries.title: Welcoming beginners and nine-hole golfers
entries.summary: Hazel Casey and others helped women gain confidence and handicaps. Phyll Sandlant’s nine-hole initiative combined Rick Barker’s professional coaching with volunteers accompanying and encouraging the newcomers.

entries.title: Nen Sim’s catering team
entries.summary: Early twilight golf depended on willing organisers and a large catering team. Mowat gives particular recognition to Nen Sim, Joan Frith, Mavis Ward and Joyce Gallagher.

entries.title: The jobs behind a convivial evening
entries.summary: Noel and Peg Copestake and their colleagues managed starts, prizes, finances, cards, barbecues, bar service and cleaning. Named helpers include Joan Brown, Bruce and Marge Anderson, Ian Dale, Peter Heeney, Steve Stephens, John Robinson, David Mowat, Des Shiel and Noeline Shiel.

entries.title: Handicapping and organisation
entries.summary: Gary Baker promoted business-house golf. David Mowat developed the twilight handicap system and software, while Peg and Kim Copestake checked and adjusted cards. The book credits the system with saving volunteer hours.

entries.title: Secretaries, subscriptions and legal work
entries.summary: Early honorary secretaries and subscription collection sustained the club. John Hare’s honorary legal work helped the Racecourse Reserve arrangements. Later paid secretary-manager roles should not all be described as unpaid work.

entries.title: Service over many seasons
entries.summary: The men’s chapter profiles years of committee, finance, match and district service. Named contributors include Warwick Nicol, Alan Davidson, Keith Frith, Maurice White, Noel Copestake, Keith Dawkins, Ernie Craig and David Mowat, as well as others who were not life members.

entries.title: Clubhouse expertise
entries.summary: Gary Baker and Tony Gallagher brought construction experience; Alan Rydings offered quantity-surveying and supervision help. Russell Black and Ismo Torvelainen were paid for professional services but also donated meeting and site-visit time. Member contractors won work through open tenders.

entries.title: Researching and preserving the history
entries.summary: Joan Mirrielees, later researchers, contributors of recollections and photographs, and Peter Steward’s veterans album preserved otherwise easily lost history. The book acknowledges veterans and the Volunteer Firewood Gang for helping finance its production.

entries.title: The people behind the scoreboards
entries.summary: Alan Davidson, Des Wilson, Jim Reid and Keith Frith gave up playing opportunities to prepare and check manually recorded results. Alex Gallagher’s calligraphy and coordination became a distinctive part of major tournaments.

entries.title: Training referees
entries.summary: The book uses an earlier disputed ruling to explain the value of trained referees, and records an enthusiastic core of qualified people following the introduction of courses in 1986. This is a historical account, not advice on present rules.

entries.title: Junior encouragement and opportunity
entries.summary: Beginners’ helpers, junior organisers and trophy donors provided pathways into golf. Ken Fraser donated the schoolboys’ Fraser Cup to encourage young players; eligibility and later administration are discussed in the book.

entries.title: Keeping tournaments going
entries.summary: Local sponsorship supported the returning professional circuit. Mowat also records officials and volunteers using squeegees in difficult weather to try to keep play moving.

entries.title: The 1968 programme’s acknowledgement
entries.summary: Noel Hayden’s acknowledgement credits the many volunteers who prepared the Masters and the advertisers whose support made the programme possible. Source: programme printed p. 48, PDF p. 50.

entries.title: Veterans’ tournament benefactors
entries.summary: Ron Galloway, John McKenzie, Gavin Wallace, Johnny Walker, Ted Bartlett and David Collins supported tournaments with cups, plates, a rose bowl, an honours board, money and prizes. Dick Phelan, George Willcock and Frank Macklow also gave trophies.

entries.title: Seats, shelter and commemorative planting
entries.summary: The book records gifts of trees, memorial seats and shelter, including Harry Butts’s seats for every tee, the Coates and Loughlin memorial seats and the shelter given in memory of Barbara Carlisle. Families and club groups helped make the grounds a place of remembrance.

entries.title: Trophies as encouragement
entries.summary: The trophy histories connect gifts with competitions and the people they encouraged. They include Mae Cameron, E. T. Baker, Bill Darley, Warwick Nicoll, Harry Bradmore, Anne Mark, Elsie Hanna, Jean Cullen, Nen Sim, Phyll Sandlant, Hazel Casey and many more.

entries.title: Community and business support
entries.summary: Donated goods, sponsorship and commercially supplied services all supported club life in different ways. Their contributions should remain identifiable rather than assuming all business work was given free.
